Los bucles anteriores suponían que el se: The previous loops assumed the sensor tells the truth. This topic begins when it does not: what is measured is the signal plus a noise that is not known. The tools are the arithmetic mean and the difference quotient from [[fn-derivadas|derivatives]], and the result is a new trade-off: the more you clean, the later you arrive.
En 1940, con Europa en guerra y los bomb: In 1940, with Europe at war and the bombing of London, Norbert Wiener was given a very concrete problem: improving the aim of anti-aircraft guns. A shell takes a few seconds to reach the aircraft's height, so you have to fire not at where the aircraft is, but at where it will be. And all that is available to guess that is a shaky radar track, full of measurement errors.
Wiener no resolvió el problema del cañón: Wiener did not solve the gun problem —the system that came out of it was never used in combat—, but in attempting it he formulated another much more general one, which turned out to be fundamental: given a signal contaminated by noise, what is the best possible estimate of the true signal, and of its future values? Out of that came the filter that bears his name, and out of that, a few years later, the whole of cybernetics.
Aquel encargo tuvo una consecuencia que: That commission had a consequence Wiener was not looking for. Working on the problem he realised that the gunner, the gun and the aircraft formed a single system with a loop, and that that loop was of the same kind as that of a person reaching out for a glass: see the deviation, correct it, look again. That leap —from ballistics to physiology— is literally the moment cybernetics was born. Wiener used to say the idea took hold in discussions with Arturo Rosenblueth, a Mexican physiologist from the Institute of Cardiology, at the scientific gatherings he organised at Harvard.
El punto de partida es una descomposició: The starting point is a decomposition that is simple to state and hard to undo: what we measure is the sum of two things.
lo medido = lo verdadero + el ruido: what is measured = what is true + the noise
Se lee: <em>«equis de te es igual a ese:
Read as: “x of t equals s of t plus n of t”.

$x(t)$ is what the device measures, $s(t)$ is the true signal we are interested in and $n(t)$ is the noise: everything that has crept in along the way.

The problem has the deceptive look of a rearrangement: $s = x - n$. But the noise is not known —if it were known, it would not be noise—, so it cannot be subtracted. It has to be estimated, and that is where the mathematics begins.
Lo que hace tratable el problema es que: What makes the problem tractable is that signal and noise usually behave differently. The signal of interest —the position of an aircraft, the temperature of a room, the price of something— changes slowly and continuously. The noise, on the other hand, jumps up and down with no memory: what it is now says nothing about what it will be the next instant.
Esa diferencia es la palanca de todo el: That difference is the lever of the whole topic. If the signal is smooth and the noise is abrupt, then averaging destroys the noise and respects the signal: on adding several consecutive values, the jumps of the noise cancel one another —some up, some down— while the signal, which has hardly changed, survives the average almost intact.
El filtro más sencillo que existe es exa: The simplest filter there is is exactly that: replacing each value by the average of the last few. It is called the moving average, and despite its simplicity it is probably the most used filter in the world.
El sombrero, $\\hat{s}$, se dice «ese es:
The hat, $\hat{s}$, is said “s estimated”: it is not the true signal, it is our approximation to it.

Read as: “s estimated sub n equals one over k, times the sum, from j equals zero to k minus one, of x sub n minus j”.

In plain words: “my estimate for now is the average of the last $k$ measured values”. The $k$ is the window, and it is the filter's only control.
Y aquí aparece el dilema que da sentido: And here appears the dilemma that gives the topic its point. The larger the window, the more noise is cancelled and the cleaner the curve comes out. But also the older: the average of the last twenty values is, in fact, an estimate of how things were ten instants ago. Smoothing costs delay, and delay, as you saw in [[cib-retardos|the topic on delays]], is what destabilises loops.

El compromiso entre suavidad y retraso: The trade-off between smoothness and delay

The thick line is what comes out of the filter. Raise the window and watch both things at once: the curve gets cleaner, and it falls behind.

Ese mando de ventana lo has usado sin sa: You have used that window control without knowing it. The 7-day moving averages of epidemic data exist to remove the weekend sawtooth, and they are why the curves in the reports were smooth while the daily figures jumped about. In the stock market, the 50- and 200-session averages are exactly this. And your phone's pedometer filters the accelerometer signal before counting a step, because otherwise it would count every tremor.
El compromiso también explica un dilema: The trade-off also explains a very real dilemma in public health and in management: smoothed data are more reliable and arrive later. Whoever decides with the seven-day average is looking at a photograph from three or four days ago; whoever decides with yesterday's figure is looking at a lot of noise. There is no universally right answer: it depends how much it costs to be wrong each way.
La media móvil que no olvida de golpe: The moving average that does not forget all at once
La media móvil de ventana $k$ tiene dos: The moving average of window $k$ has two practical drawbacks. You have to store the last $k$ values, and the one that drops off the back disappears at a stroke: a figure has the same influence for $k$ steps and then none. There is a variant that stores nothing and forgets gradually, and it is the one most used.
Se lee: <em>«ese sub ene es beta por ese:
Read as: “s sub n is beta times s sub n minus one, plus one minus beta times x sub n”.

Each new value enters with weight $1-\beta$ and everything earlier shrinks by being multiplied by $\beta$. Unfolding the recurrence, the figure from $k$ steps ago weighs $(1-\beta)\beta^k$: a [[fn-sucesiones|geometric progression]] of ratio $\beta$, whose weights add up to exactly 1.

There is no window to store: one number, $s_{n-1}$, is enough. The effective memory is about $\frac{1}{1-\beta}$ values, so $\beta = 0{.}9$ remembers about ten and $\beta = 0{.}99$, about a hundred.
Fíjate en que esto es <strong>el bucle d: Notice that this is the loop from the first topic again: written as $s_n = s_{n-1} + (1-\beta)(x_n - s_{n-1})$, it is a correction proportional to the error with gain $K = 1-\beta$, exactly that of [[cib-realimentacion|feedback]]. A filter and a regulator are the same equation looked at from two places.
Esa media móvil tiene un nombre general: That moving average has a general name and a whole family behind it. Sliding a list of weights over a signal, multiplying and adding at each position, is a [[av-convolucion|convolution]]: with equal weights out comes this average, with other weights out comes a smoothing that respects steps better, and with weights adding up to zero out comes a change detector instead of a smoother.
El paso siguiente, y el que de verdad in: The next step, and the one Wiener really cared about, is the most ambitious. If the filter serves to estimate where something is, why not use the same information to estimate where it will be?
La idea básica es sorprendentemente acce: The basic idea is surprisingly accessible with what you already know: if to the estimated position you add the estimated velocity multiplied by the time your action will take, you get a forecast. And estimating the velocity from the measurements is computing a derivative, which is exactly what you know how to do.
predecir es extrapolar con la derivada: predicting is extrapolating with the derivative
El símbolo $\\approx$ se lee «aproximada:
The symbol $\approx$ is read “approximately equal”. $\Delta$ is the Greek capital delta and here it is the time you want to look ahead by.

It is said: “s estimated of t plus delta is approximately s estimated of t, plus the derivative of s estimated at t, times delta”.

You will recognise the formula: it is the tangent line from [[fn-derivadas|derivatives]], used as a crystal ball. It assumes that for a little while the signal will carry on with the same gradient it has.
Por qué derivar es peligroso con datos r: Why differentiating is dangerous with noisy data
Antes de seguir hace falta justificar al: Before going on, something usually dropped in as if it were obvious has to be justified: that the derivative amplifies noise. With one number it is seen at once.
Supón que mides cada centésima de segund: Suppose you measure every hundredth of a second, that is $\Delta t = 0{.}01$, and that your sensor has an error of barely a tenth of a unit. Two consecutive measurements can differ by $0{.}2$ through noise alone —one drifts up and the next down—. On estimating the derivative as a difference quotient, that error is divided by the step:
una décima de ruido, veinte de derivada: a tenth of noise, twenty of false derivative
La cuenta es la del cociente incremental:
The computation is that of the difference quotient: change divided by time elapsed.

What matters is where the disaster comes from: the noise is not divided, it is multiplied by $1/\Delta t$. And $\Delta t$ is small precisely because we want to measure often. The faster you measure, the worse: with a step of one millisecond, that same tenth of noise produces a false derivative of 200.
Fíjate en la ironía: medir más a menudo: Notice the irony: measuring more often improves the estimate of the position and worsens that of the velocity. The true signal hardly changes in a hundredth of a second, so its contribution to the numerator is minute; the noise, on the other hand, jumps the same regardless of the step. In the quotient, the noise wins hands down.
Y aquí está la tensión que hace difícil: And here is the tension that makes the problem hard, and the reason a Wiener was needed. To predict you need the derivative of the signal; but the derivative amplifies noise, as you have just seen, so first you have to smooth; and smoothing introduces delay, which is precisely what you wanted to compensate for by predicting. The three things pull against one another, and the Wiener filter is the optimal answer to that tug of war when the statistical properties of the signal and the noise are known.
La pescadilla que se muerde la cola: The snake biting its own tail
Wiener publicó su solución en 1942 en un: Wiener published his solution in 1942 in a yellow-covered military report the engineers nicknamed the yellow peril for the arduousness of its mathematics. It was declassified in 1949. Shortly after, in 1960, Rudolf Kálmán published a different and far more practical formulation, which could be computed step by step and worked in changing systems: the Kalman filter. NASA adopted it for the Apollo programme, and the navigation of the Moon missions was done with it. Today it goes inside every satnav, every drone and every car that locates itself in a lane.
Cuando el GPS de tu móvil te sitúa en la: When your phone's GPS places you on the right street even though the satellite signal arrives with errors of several metres, what is happening is exactly this: a filter combines the noisy measurements with a model of how you move —that you cannot teleport, that you have a velocity— and produces an estimate better than either of the two alone. That is why the blue dot goes on advancing reasonably for a few seconds even if you enter a tunnel: it is predicting.
